title: Subscription Lifecycle
description: Master subscription lifecycle events, cleanup patterns, and error handling in Apollo Client.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Subscription Lifecycle**. Master subscription lifecycle events, cleanup patterns, and error handling in Apollo Client. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Subscription Lifecycle and be confident in applying it to your projects.
Subscription Lifecycle Events

When you call `useSubscription`, Apollo Client establishes the WebSocket connection if needed, sends the subscription payload, and then waits for the server to push results. The hook exposes callbacks for the key events in this lifecycle.

items: onSubscriptionData: Fires when the server pushes new data
onError: Fires when the server sends an error or the connection fails
onComplete: Fires when the server signals the subscription stream is done
data.title: Primary Lifecycle Callbacks
Lifecycle Callbacks

data.text: Automatic Cleanup

React hooks handle cleanup automatically. When a component using `useSubscription` unmounts, Apollo Client sends an unsubscribe message to the server and removes the listener. This prevents memory leaks and stray network traffic.

data.title: Automatic Unmount Cleanup
data.content: No manual cleanup needed with hooks

data.title: Avoid Manual Subscriptions in useEffect
data.text: Do not use `client.subscribe()` inside useEffect unless you absolutely need to. The hook manages the lifecycle correctly. Manual subscriptions require explicit `unsubscribe()` calls and are error-prone.
Error Handling

Subscription errors fall into two categories: transport errors (network drops, invalid auth) and GraphQL errors (invalid payload, server exception). The `onError` callback receives both, but you should differentiate them to provide the right user experience.

data.title: Differentiating Error Types

data.text: Retry and Backoff

Some subscription errors are transient. For example, a brief server overload might return a 503. You can implement retry logic by stopping and restarting the subscription, or by using the `graphql-ws` retry configuration.

data.title: Exponential Backoff Retry
Server-Side Cleanup
data.text: Always clean up server-side subscription resolvers when the client disconnects. Failing to do so causes memory leaks on the server and may exhaust connection limits. Use the `onComplete` callback or WebSocket close events to trigger server cleanup.

data.caption: State transitions during a subscription lifecycle
data.definition:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Connecting: Component mounts
    Connecting --> Subscribed: Connection ack + GQL subscribe
    Subscribed --> Receiving: onSubscriptionData
    Receiving --> Receiving: New event
    Receiving --> Erroring: onError
    Erroring --> Reconnecting: Network error + retry enabled
    Erroring --> Completed: Non-retryable error
    Reconnecting --> Subscribed: Reconnect success
    Subscribed --> Completed: onComplete / unmount
    Completed --> [*]

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: useSubscription handles mount and unmount automatically
onSubscriptionData, onError, and onComplete cover the main lifecycle events
Differentiate transport errors from GraphQL errors for better UX
Retry failed subscriptions with exponential backoff for resilience
data.takeaway: Understanding the lifecycle prevents memory leaks and builds resilient real-time features.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **Subscription Lifecycle**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of Subscription Lifecycle when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Subscription Lifecycle**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Subscription Lifecycle**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
